Title: Blindness and visual impairment and their causes in India: Results of a nationally representative survey
Authors: Praveen Vashist; Suraj Singh Senjam; Vivek Gupta; Noopur Gupta; B. R. Shamanna; Meenakshi Wadhwani; Pallavi Shukla; Souvik Manna; Saumya Yadav; Amit Bharadwaj
Research area: Epidemiology of vision loss in India (National Blindness & Visual Impairment Survey 2015-19)
Problem addressed: Need national estimates of blindness/VI and causes in India.
Target population: 85,135 people aged >= 50 examined (93,018 enumerated) in 31 districts.
Methodology: Cross-sectional RAAB v6 survey, weighted and age/sex standardised.
Main findings: Blindness prevalence 1.99% in people >= 50; more than a quarter of people >= 50 visually impaired (<6/12); cataract 66.2% of blindness; 92.9% of blindness avoidable; older age and illiteracy associated with blindness; extrapolated ~4.8 million blind people (all ages) in 2017.
Limitations: Survey of >= 50 years only; avoidable causes dominate.
Relevance to SPARSH: India-specific need statement; also implies many blind users are older and possibly not braille-literate -> supports shape code over braille.
Design implications: Design for older, late-blind, low-literacy users: larger symbols (x1.5 per ISO 24508 for older users), no braille dependency, Hindi/regional-language caregiver guide.

Title: World Report on Vision
Main findings: At least 2.2 billion people have vision impairment or blindness, of whom at least 1 billion have preventable or unaddressed impairment; blindness rates in South Asia about eight times those of high-income countries.

Title: IS 3854: Switches for domestic and similar purposes / Switches for household and similar fixed electrical installations - Part 1: General requirements
Main findings: Covers manually operated general-purpose switches up to 440 V and 63 A for household fixed installations; closely aligned with IEC 60669-1; requires ISI mark. No tactile/accessibility marking found in the summaries.
Limitations: Full text not read; ON/OFF marking clause not verified.
Relevance to SPARSH: Defines the physical object SPARSH caps fit (Indian modular rocker switches); caps must not interfere with switch operation or safety.
Design implications: Caps must not cover ventilation/terminals, must not require removing switch plates, and must be non-conductive (PLA/PETG/TPU).

Title: IS 1293: Plugs and socket-outlets of rated voltage up to and including 250 V and rated current up to and including 16 A
DOI/URL: BIS catalogue; summary: infralens.in/code/IS-1293-2019; full 2005 text on law.resource.org (not read)
Main findings: Covers plugs and socket-outlets up to 250 V, 16 A (6 A and 16 A Type D configurations with different pin geometry), mandatory shutters; largely harmonised with IEC 60884-1. No tactile features found.
Relevance to SPARSH: Socket caps must leave pin holes and shutters fully unobstructed.
Design implications: Place socket triangle on the adjacent socket switch, not on the socket face.

Title: The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 (Act No. 49 of 2016)
Journal/conference: Act of Parliament; assent 27 December 2016; Gazette 28 December 2016
Main findings: Sec. 40: Central Government sets accessibility standards; Sec. 42: everyday electronic goods to be available in universal design; Sec. 43: promote universally designed consumer products; Sec. 44-46: compliance and timelines. Universal design defined as design of products, environments, programmes and services usable by all people to the greatest extent possible, incl. assistive devices.
Limitations: Mandates focus on public infrastructure/services rather than private homes.
Relevance to SPARSH: Policy hook: SPARSH as a universally designed, low-cost consumer retrofit (Sec. 42-43).

Title: Harmonised Guidelines and Standards for Universal Accessibility in India 2021
Authors: Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA), Government of India
Target population: All users incl. persons with disabilities.
Main findings: Sec. 4.15: operable controls 600-1200 mm above floor (washroom light switches 800-1200 mm); sockets/switches >= 350 mm from internal corners; switch plate to contrast with wall by >= 30 points LRV; controls illuminable to >= 100 lux; one-hand operation, force 2.5-5 N; tactile button alternative to touch controls. Residential (6.1.7): interior controls 900-1200 mm. Secured-entry controls (7.4): raised buttons with high contrast, raised numerals/letters.
Limitations: No requirement for tactile identification of what each switch controls.
Relevance to SPARSH: Indian design baseline for switches; shows national guidance covers reach, contrast and force but not tactile function identification.
Design implications: Caps must keep operating force within ~2.5-5 N (no added stiffness); use a contrasting cap colour (benefits low-vision users, cf. 30 LRV); keep caps from protruding into neighbouring switches.
